# Types & the Output Contract

**Source:** `crates/core/src/types/output.rs`, `crates/core/src/types/diagnostic.rs`, `crates/core/src/types/collected.rs`, `crates/core/src/types/global.rs`, `crates/core/src/react_types.rs`

This is the data shared between every phase of the pipeline (`OXC parse → SourceData (extractor) → GlobalSourceData (pipeline) → ComponentEntry (resolver) → ExtractionOutput`). These types _are_ the contract: extractor and resolver code on either side of a phase boundary only agree on behavior because they agree on these shapes.

## The two-representation split

There are two recursive "type" enums, one per side of the resolver boundary:

- `CollectedType` (`types/collected.rs`) — the extractor's raw, unresolved AST-level representation. Still has TypeScript-shaped variants: `Conditional`, `Mapped`, `TypeOf`, `KeyOf`, `IndexedAccess`, `TemplateLiteral`, `Raw`.
- `PropType` (`types/output.rs`) — the resolver's fully-resolved semantic output. TypeScript-shaped ambiguity has been resolved away or converted to `PropType::Opaque` with a reason.

`resolver/` pattern-matches `CollectedType` to produce `PropType`; nothing downstream of the resolver ever sees a `CollectedType` again.

```rust
pub enum CollectedType {
    String, Number, Boolean, Null, Undefined, Any, Never, Unknown, Void, BigInt, Symbol,
    StringLiteral(CompactString), NumberLiteral(f64), BoolLiteral(bool),
    Union(Vec<CollectedType>), Intersection(Vec<CollectedType>), Array(Box<CollectedType>),
    Tuple(Vec<CollectedType>), Object(Vec<CollectedObjectField>),
    Named { name: CompactString, args: Vec<CollectedType> },
    TypeOf(CompactString),
    KeyOf(Box<CollectedType>),
    AtFile { file: Utf8PathBuf, inner: Box<CollectedType> },
    IndexedAccess { obj: Box<CollectedType>, key: Box<CollectedType> },
    TemplateLiteral(Vec<CollectedType>),
    Function { params: Vec<CollectedType>, param_names: Vec<Option<CompactString>>, return_type: Box<CollectedType> },
    Conditional { check: Box<CollectedType>, extends_type: Box<CollectedType>, true_type: Box<CollectedType>, false_type: Box<CollectedType> },
    Mapped { key_type: Box<CollectedType>, value_type: Box<CollectedType> },
    Raw(std::string::String),
}
```

```rust
pub enum PropType {
    String, Number, Boolean, Null, Undefined, Any, Never, Unknown, Void,
    StringLiteral(String), NumberLiteral(f64), BoolLiteral(bool),
    Union(Vec<PropType>), Intersection(Vec<PropType>), Array(Box<PropType>),
    Tuple(Vec<PropType>), Object(Vec<ObjectField>),
    Named { name: TypeName, args: Vec<PropType> },
    ReactNode, CssProperties,
    Function { type_params: Vec<String>, params: Vec<FunctionParam>, return_type: Box<PropType> }, // FunctionParam: name, type, optional, rest
    Ref { element: Option<String> },
    ElementType,
    HtmlAttributes { element: String, omitted: Vec<String> },
    LiteralUnion { members: Vec<String>, has_default: bool },
    SxProps,
    Opaque(OpaqueDetail),
}
```

Note what disappeared crossing the boundary: `BigInt`, `Symbol`, `TypeOf`, `KeyOf`, `AtFile`, `IndexedAccess`, `TemplateLiteral`, `Function`, `Conditional`, `Mapped`, `Raw` are all gone from `PropType`. Each either resolves into a concrete `PropType` variant (`Function` becomes `PropType::Function` with its parameters and return type resolved) or terminates in `PropType::Opaque` with an `OpaqueReason` explaining exactly which unresolvable TypeScript construct it was (`ConditionalType`, `MappedType`, `IndexedAccess`, `TemplateLiteral`, ...). This is the resolver's entire job, structurally: eliminate every "can't be sure yet" variant.

## LOCKED DESIGN DECISION: manual Serialize/Deserialize on the recursive enums (ADR-0002)

**Source:** `docs/adr/0002-manual-serialize-for-prop-type.md`

`PropType` and `CollectedType` do **not** derive `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Both implement the serde traits by hand. `CollectedType` (`crates/core/src/types/collected.rs`) round-trips through a private `to_json_value`/`from_json_value` pair that builds and reads a `serde_json::Value`. `PropType` (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`) streams its `Serialize` impl straight into the serializer as a map with `kind` first and the fields in a fixed order (an `OpaqueReason` is written by the private `WireReason` as `{ type, ... }`), and deserializes through a private `from_tagged_value` over a `serde_json::Value`.

**Why:** these are recursive enums (`Union(Vec<Self>)`, `Object(Vec<Field>)` where `Field` contains `Self`, `Array(Box<Self>)`, ...). A derived, tagged (`#[serde(tag = "kind")]`) implementation on a recursive enum needed `#![recursion_limit = "2048"]` to compile — each nesting level wraps the generated (de)serializer in another codegen layer, and a real component prop tree blows past the default limit (128). Manual impls sidestep the codegen recursion entirely; they're just recursive Rust functions, which the compiler doesn't limit the same way.

**Do not "simplify" this back to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`.** It looks removable — it's a lot of boilerplate for something serde could theoretically generate — but doing so reintroduces the recursion-limit dependency, and worse, silently drops the manual NaN/Infinity handling described below.

**Correction to the ADR itself, verified against current code:** ADR-0002 states "`PropType`, `CollectedType`, and `OpaqueReason` don't derive Serialize/Deserialize." This is stale for `OpaqueReason`. The current source (`OpaqueReason` in `types/output.rs`) shows:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub enum OpaqueReason {
    ConditionalType, MappedType, ModuleAugmentation,
    RuntimeDependent { function_name: String },
    UnresolvableImport { specifier: String },
    PandaCodegenMissing, DepthExceeded,
    IndexedAccess { expression: String },
    TemplateLiteral { expression: String },
    UnsupportedExpression,
}
```

`OpaqueReason` derives normally. It isn't recursive — every variant's payload is a `String` or a unit — so it never hit the recursion-limit problem the ADR is about. The _serialization of an `OpaqueReason` value_ is still hand-assembled by `WireReason` (`types/output.rs`, matching each reason to its own `{ type, ... }` shape) when `PropType`'s `Serialize` writes the `Opaque` variant, and hand-parsed in `PropType::from_tagged_value` — but that's because it's embedded inside `PropType`'s own manual impl, not because `OpaqueReason` itself needs one. This is a small, real documentation bug in ADR-0002 worth a one-line fix, independent of anything else in this file.

Also worth noting as **resolved, not a gap:** the ADR flagged `#![recursion_limit = "2048"]` in `lib.rs` as "left over from the old derive-based design... worth deleting as a follow-up." As of the current source, `crates/core/src/lib.rs` has no `recursion_limit` attribute at all — that follow-up has already happened. The ADR's "Consequences" section is stale on this point too.

### The "no wildcard matches" convention

**Invariant 1:** Every match on `PropType` or `CollectedType` inside the manual serde impls, and by extension idiomatically everywhere else in the resolver, must be exhaustive — no `_ => ...` fallthrough arm.

**Why it's load-bearing:** a derived serde impl gives you a compiler error the moment you add a new enum variant and forget to handle it in serialization. A hand-written match loses that safety net _unless every match stays exhaustive_ — a wildcard arm would silently absorb a new variant into whatever the wildcard does (often `Opaque` or a panic), and nothing would tell you serialization is now lossy for that variant. `PropType`'s `Serialize` impl and `from_tagged_value` (`types/output.rs`), and `to_json_value`/`from_json_value` in `collected.rs`, are all written this way. If you add a `PropType` variant, the compiler _will_ fail the exhaustiveness check in the `Serialize` impl and force you to handle it — but only because nobody put a wildcard there. Adding one defeats the entire safety mechanism this ADR relies on.

### NaN/Infinity as a wire-format special case

**Invariant 2:** `PropType::NumberLiteral(f64)` and `CollectedType::NumberLiteral(f64)` encode non-finite values (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`) as JSON strings (`"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`), not as JSON numbers, and the read side must check for a string before falling back to `as_f64()`.

**Why:** `serde_json::Number` (and JSON itself) cannot represent non-finite floats — `serde_json::json!(f64::NAN)` silently becomes `null`. Without the string-tag workaround, a `NumberLiteral(NaN)` would round-trip as `0.0` (the comments in `PropType`'s `Serialize` impl and in `CollectedType::to_json_value`) or, in `CollectedType`'s case, fail every match arm in `from_json_value` and fall through to `Raw`. Both files have explicit round-trip tests for this (`number_literal_roundtrip_tests` in `output.rs`, the NaN/Infinity/-Infinity tests in `collected.rs`'s `mod tests`) — treat those as regression guards, not optional coverage.

1	# Serialization formats
2	
3	**Source:** `crates/core/src/pipeline/rdt.rs` (`serialize`, `docgen_info`, `type_json`, `omits`), `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs` (`serialize_rdt`), `crates/core/src/toon.rs` (whole module), `crates/cli/src/commands/schema.rs` (`schema_value`, `cmd_schema`, its drift test), `crates/core/src/types/output.rs` (`PropType::is_literal_union`), `crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs` (`ResolvedChain::give_up`, `empty_with_compose`)
4	
5	This tool's canonical, lossless representation is `ExtractionOutput` — the struct tree in `crates/core/src/types/`, whose JSON writes each distinct prop once and refers to it by id (ADR 0009; see `types-and-output-contract.md`). Everything in this document is a _consumer-facing projection_ of that canonical form: two formats reshape it for specific downstream tools (`--format rdt`, `--format toon`), and one (`schema.rs`) describes its shape for external validators. None of the three is the source of truth; `ExtractionOutput` is.
6	
7	## Schema version
8	
9	The canonical JSON (`ExtractionOutput`, `IncrementalUpdate`, the session index) carries `schemaVersion` (ADR 0017); `SCHEMA_VERSION` in `crates/core/src/types/output.rs` is the one definition, and `schema.rs` requires it. Version 1 is the shape ADR 0009 describes. Version 2 (ADR 0018) writes a component's `props` as prop set ids, and an inheritance layer's `omitted` and a diagnostic's `affects` as name list ids, with `propSets` and `nameLists` tables beside `props`. Version 3 adds `optional` and `rest` to a function type's parameters, written only when true, and lists a rest parameter as the last parameter. OXC keeps `...rest` apart from the other parameters and the extractor read only the others, so `(...args: any[]) => void` printed as `() => void` and `(a?: string) => void` as `(a: string) => void`; a caller reading the signature believed an argument was required or that none were accepted. It is a bump, not an addition a reader can ignore: a version 2 reader would show `...args: any[]` as a required parameter named `args`. `raw_string` prints `a?: T` and `...a: T[]` as RDT does, TOON prints `T?` and `...T`, and `structural_hash` includes both flags. The TypeScript 7.1 backend does not set them: `crates/semantic/src/convert.rs` builds every parameter as required. Version 4 keeps three things the output used to drop, and is one bump because a version 3 reader would misread each: `readonly`, index signatures and the ref type's name. `readonly string[]` and `readonly [A, B]` are `{ "kind": "readonly", "element": … }` around the array or tuple (`PropType::Readonly`, `CollectedType::Readonly`); a union keeps `string[] | readonly string[]` as two members, since they are two types. An object field gains `readonly` (written only when true) for `readonly name: T`, and `indexKey` (written only for an index signature) for `[name: K]: T`: such a field is `name` the key parameter, `propType` the value and `indexKey` the key type. An index signature is not a prop, so everything that reads an object's fields as props, keys or lookup targets skips a field with `indexKey` (`is_member`), and a props type with only an index signature lists no props. `ref` gains `name`, the React type as written without `React.` (`Ref`, `RefObject`, `ForwardedRef`, `MutableRefObject`, `RefCallback`, `LegacyRef`, `ElementRef`), and `raw_string` prints `RefObject<T>` rather than `Ref<T>`. `declare const X: readonly ["a", "b"]` is still read as the tuple (`record_declared_value_type` peels the operator). The Vite plugin and the Storybook addon read version 4 only, and an old parse cache is discarded once (`CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` in `cache.rs`). The TypeScript 7.1 backend sets none of them: `crates/semantic/src/convert.rs` builds every object field as a plain, writable member and has no `readonly` or ref conversion. Not carried: `readonly` on a component's own props (a `readonly label: string` member of a props interface), which no consumer reads yet. A collapsed inheritance layer (`docs/architecture/resolver-type-resolution.md`, Collapse) also names the props it holds: `InheritedLayer.members`, written as the id of a list in `nameLists` (so a source shared by many components is written once) and only for a layer that has members. It is an addition a reader can ignore, so it did not move `SCHEMA_VERSION`; a reader that wants to know whether a prop collapsed away or is absent reads it.
10	
11	- **Bump** when a reader of the previous version would misread or lose data: a field removed, renamed or retyped, its meaning changed, or references and tables restructured. A new field, a new `detectedBy` value or a new diagnostic code is not a bump; readers must tolerate them.
12	- **A bump ships** in a changeset marked breaking for the core crate and every package that reads the JSON.
13	- **Readers** (`ExtractionOutput`'s `Deserialize`, `packages/vite-plugin/src/schema.ts`, `packages/storybook/src/schema.ts`) accept their own version, reject any other with an error naming both, and read output with no `schemaVersion` as version 1.
14	- `--format rdt`, `--format storybook` and `--format toon` carry no version; they have other tools' shapes. The parse cache has its own `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`.
15	
16	## Where this code lives, and why that's not a AGENTS.md violation
17	
18	`crates/core/AGENTS.md` says "no terminal/display code in `crates/core`." The RDT projection (`pipeline/rdt.rs`) and `toon.rs` (`render_output_toon`, `render_component_toon`, `format_type_compact`) live in **`crates/core`**, and both are serialization formats, not extraction logic.
19	
20	The line the project actually draws, reverse-engineered from where each format lives: "terminal/display code" means code whose job is to _render for a human looking at a terminal_ (colors, tables, spinners — `crates/cli/src/output.rs`'s comfy-table helpers, `indicatif` progress bars). A _serialization format_ — even a human-readable, LLM-optimized one like TOON — is a consumer-facing data contract, judged by "does another program or prompt consume this," not "is it pretty-printed." TOON is core-side because it's plumbed through `PipelineOptions`/pipeline output the same way canonical JSON is (`caliper_docgen_core::toon::render_output_toon(&output)` called from `cmd_extract` in `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs`), and because a NAPI/plugin consumer could plausibly want TOON output too, not just the CLI. The RDT shape is core-side for the same reason: the NAPI binding's `sessionDocgenInfo` returns it per component for the Storybook provider (`packages/storybook`), and `--format rdt` (`serialize_rdt`) delegates to the same module.
21	
22	**Invariant 1:** A new serialization format belongs in `crates/core` only if a non-CLI consumer (NAPI binding, a plugin, a future query server) could plausibly want to produce it directly from a `PipelineOptions`/`ExtractionOutput` value. If a format exists solely to match another CLI tool's file-format contract, it belongs in `crates/cli/src/commands/`, not `crates/core`.
23	
24	## RDT format (`pipeline::rdt`)
25	
26	Two entry points share one projection: `serialize` (`--format rdt`) applies RDT's default `skipChildrenPropWithoutDoc` (`omits`), and `docgen_info` (the NAPI `sessionDocgenInfo`, feeding the Storybook provider) keeps an undocumented `children`, because Storybook 11's React docgen lists it.
27	
28	`serialize` holds only components with `exported: true`, unless `--include-unexported` is passed. react-docgen-typescript documents only a module's exports, so a file-local helper component would otherwise appear in RDT-shaped output where RDT never puts one.
29	
30	Each component `serialize` writes carries `filePath`, the absolute path of its source file, as RDT's `ComponentDoc` does. `docgen_info` leaves it out.
31	
32	### The `enum`-shape convention (`type_json`)
33	
34	react-docgen-typescript encodes a literal union prop type not as an inlined string but as a structured shape renderers pattern-match on:
35	
36	```rust
37	if prop_type.is_literal_union() {
38	    let values: Vec<serde_json::Value> = match prop_type {
39	        PropType::Union(members) => members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": m.raw_string()})).collect(),
40	        PropType::LiteralUnion { members, .. } => {
41	            members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": format!("\"{m}\"")})).collect()
42	        }
43	        single => vec![serde_json::json!({"value": single.raw_string()})],
44	    };
45	    return serde_json::json!({ "name": "enum", "raw": prop_type.raw_string(), "value": values });
46	}
47	serde_json::json!({ "name": prop_type.raw_string() })
48	```
49	
50	A single string or number literal (`kind?: 'button'`) is a one-option `enum`, which is what Storybook's own docgen produces for it. A union with a boolean member (`'a' | 1 | true`) is not an `enum`: Storybook unquotes each option's source text into a string or a number, so `true` would reach the control as the string `"true"`. It stays a type name, `{"name": "\"a\" | 1 | true"}`, which Storybook's converter splits at the `|` and parses as JSON itself, giving the options `["a", 1, true]` with a real boolean (its own docgen gives such a union no options at all). That holds only while every member's text survives the split and parse: a string holding `|`, `"` or `\` (`'a|b' | true`) is split inside the literal or fails `JSON.parse` (`'a\\b'` parses to a backspace), and Storybook then picks an `object` control. Such a union is an `enum` as before (`true` is then the string "true"), so that no option is lost.
51	
52	This exists because Storybook's own docgen addon (a real consumer of RDT's JSON) looks for `type.name === "enum"` as the trigger to render a `<select>` control instead of a free-text field — the single highest-value renderer hook for the most commonly curated kind of prop in any design system (`variant`, `size`, `color`, …).
53	
54	**Invariant 2:** `rdt::type_json` returns `{"name": "enum", "raw": ..., "value": [...]}` if and only if `prop_type.is_literal_union()` is `true`. Do not special-case `PropType::Union`/`PropType::LiteralUnion` shape-matching directly inside `rdt::type_json` — route every literal-union check through `is_literal_union()`, because that's the single place that rule (below) is enforced.
55	
56	### Which types are `enum`s
57	
58	`PropType::is_literal_union()` (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`) is true for a non-empty `Union` whose members are all string or number literals, a `Union` of literals with at least one string or number and a boolean whose text Storybook cannot split and parse from the type name (`reads_as_json_options`), a non-empty `LiteralUnion`, and a lone string or number literal (a bare `StringLiteral`/`NumberLiteral`).
59	
60	**Invariant 3:** A `PropType::Union`/`PropType::LiteralUnion` with **0** members, and a union of booleans only (a lone `true` included), is never reported as an `enum` shape. An empty "enum" (`{"name": "enum", "value": []}`) is misleading to a prop-table renderer, and a zero-member `LiteralUnion` is still reachable (if cosmetic) from several construction paths (`known.rs`, `resolver/primitives.rs`, `resolver/alias.rs`, `resolver/mod.rs`, `resolver/template.rs`); the guard in `is_literal_union()` keeps that from surfacing as a broken `enum` shape in RDT output, where it degrades to a plain `{"name": raw_string()}`. A single string or number literal is an enum: before, it was written as a type name, and Storybook picked an `object` control for a prop that is only ever `'button'`.
61	
62	### `@ignore`
63	
64	`component_doc` leaves out a prop whose tags hold `ignore`, in both `serialize` and `docgen_info`, because Storybook's own docgen (`@storybook/react`'s `react-component-meta` path) drops `@ignore` props and no other tag (`@internal`, `@private`, `@hidden` and `@deprecated` props are all listed). The canonical output keeps the prop and its tag.
65	
66	### `composes` reused for the resolver's give-up cases
67	
68	RDT natively supports a `composes: string[]` field on each component — "these props come from this named type, listed by reference, not flattened into `props`." This tool's resolver reuses that exact mechanism for a second, distinct purpose: recording every type it gave up trying to resolve. `ResolvedChain::give_up` (`crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs`) is "the sanctioned 'give up' entry point for every 'this type couldn't be followed further, stop here' path" — it pushes an optional `Diagnostic` and then calls `empty_with_compose(type_name)`, which sets `composes: vec![type_name]`. Every unresolvable type (a conditional type, a generic pattern the resolver doesn't understand, a cycle) lands in `composes` instead of silently vanishing from `props`.
69	
70	`rdt::docgen_info` passes `entry.composes` straight through (`"composes": entry.composes`) — this was previously a real bug (see `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs`'s `rdt_output_includes_composes` test and its docstring): the resolver populated `composes` correctly but `serialize_rdt` silently dropped it from the emitted JSON. Fixed; the field now round-trips.
71	
72	**Invariant 4:** `composes` in the emitted RDT JSON carries two semantically different populations that are _not_ distinguished from each other in the output: (a) types RDT itself would put there — legitimate "props come from elsewhere" composition, and (b) types this resolver gave up resolving. A consumer reading `composes` cannot tell which case produced a given entry without re-running extraction and checking `diagnostics` for a correlated warning. Do not "clean up" `give_up` to stop populating `composes`, and do not add a second field to split the two populations without updating this doc and `resolver-type-resolution.md` — the reuse is intentional (see that file for the resolver-side rationale), not an accident that happens to also serialize correctly.
73	
74	**Cross-reference:** the resolver-side mechanics of `give_up`/`empty_with_compose`/cycle detection belong to `resolver-type-resolution.md`, not here — this file only documents the serialization-format consequence (the field showing up in RDT JSON), not the resolution logic that populates it.
75	
76	### `ref`/`key`: deliberate omission, not a bug, not relocated
77	
78	RDT lists React's `ref` and `key` reconciliation props alongside a component's real props. This tool does not. `docs/benchmarks.md` documents this precisely: of components with any prop-count mismatch against real RDT, "the other 24 (0.9%, spread across 12 of the other 23 components) are **100% `ref`/`key`**... Worth being precise about that one: it's an omission, not a relocation — this tool doesn't surface forwardRef/ref-type metadata anywhere else either (checked `ComponentEntry`'s full field list — no such field exists), so 'we chose not to add it' is accurate, but 'the same info lives elsewhere' isn't."
79	
80	**Invariant 5:** Neither `ref` nor `key` appears in `props`, in any other `ComponentEntry` field, or in any of the serialization formats in this document. If a future change adds `ref`-as-prop support (React 19's `function Button({ ref, ...props })` pattern — see `docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s "React 19 `ref`-as-prop" note, already investigated and found to already work structurally when `ref` is an explicit member of the props type), that is a change to what the _resolver_ extracts, not a serialization-format decision — this document's job is only to record that today, none of the formats invent `ref`/`key` entries that the canonical `ExtractionOutput` doesn't already contain.
81	
82	### `methods: []` — always empty, and why RDT/Storybook both still carry the field
83	
84	**Locked design decision:** `rdt::docgen_info` hardcodes `"methods": []` unconditionally rather than omitting the field or computing it. This tool does not extract class component methods — "this tool doesn't extract class methods, and RDT consumers (Storybook's docgen addon) only ever read it for class components". Since class components are explicitly out of scope for this project (`docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s Component patterns table: `Class component | ❌ | out of scope (modern React only)`), the field is kept present-but-empty rather than dropped, because RDT/Storybook consumers may assume the key always exists on a valid RDT-shaped component entry — dropping it risks a `TypeError` on `.methods.length` in a consumer that doesn't defensively check for the key's presence, whereas an empty array is always safe to iterate.
85	
86	## TOON format (`crates/core/src/toon.rs`)
87	
88	TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) is a compact, indentation-and-CSV-like text encoding for `ExtractionOutput`, designed for LLM prompt/agent-context consumption rather than for a program to parse back into structured data.
89	
90	### It is deliberately lossy — not meant to round-trip
91	
92	**Locked design decision:** TOON output is not a serialization format in the reversible sense. It:
93	
94	- Collapses `PropType` into a single compact string per prop (`format_type_compact`) — e.g. `Array<string>`, `Ref<HTMLButtonElement>`, `(event: MouseEvent) => void`, `opaque(CustomType)` — discarding structure a JSON consumer would get from the tagged `PropType` enum (no way to tell from the string alone whether `SxProps` came from `PropType::SxProps` vs. a `Named` type happening to render the same text).
95	- Escapes only for CSV-safety (`escape_toon_val`: commas, newlines, quotes) — not for full round-trip fidelity.
96	- Truncates a union of types (more than 8 members), an intersection (more than 4) and a collapsed layer's `members` (more than 24), replacing the tail with a `"...(+N)"` marker; the canonical JSON holds every member. It never cuts a literal union or a union with a literal member, because an agent writes a call from those values. A function type keeps its parameter names. A prop's `@deprecated`, `@see` and `@since` tags are written in a `tags` column (present only when some prop has one), and a discriminated union's discriminant prop in a `discriminant:` line.
97	
98	There is no `parse_toon` / deserializer anywhere in the codebase, and none is planned — TOON is a one-way export.
99	
100	**Invariant 7:** No code path may treat TOON output as re-parseable back into `ExtractionOutput` or any `PropType`. If a future feature needs a compact-but-lossless format, that is a new format, not an extension of TOON's contract.
101	
102	### Truncation with a required indicator — recently made consistent
103	
104	`truncate_with_indicator(parts: &[String], limit: usize, sep: &str) -> String` (`crates/core/src/toon.rs`) is the single shared helper for "cut a member list down to `limit` items, and if anything was cut, say so":
105	
106	```rust
107	fn truncate_with_indicator(parts: &[String], limit: usize, sep: &str) -> String {
108	    if parts.len() <= limit {
109	        return parts.join(sep);
110	    }
111	    let mut shown: Vec<String> = parts[..limit].to_vec();
112	    shown.push(format!("...(+{})", parts.len() - limit));
113	    shown.join(sep)
114	}
115	```
116	
117	Three call sites route through it, each with its own cap: `Union` of types only (`UNION_LIMIT` 8, separator `|`; a union with a string, number or boolean literal member is written in full), `Intersection` (limit 4, separator `&`) and a layer's `members` (limit 24). `LiteralUnion` is not cut.
118	
119	This was a real, confirmed bug before the fix: `LiteralUnion`'s truncate-with-indicator logic existed but was never factored into a shared helper, so when `Union`/`Intersection` needed the same behavior _in the same function_ (`format_type_compact`), the indicator half was silently dropped — those two branches truncated the member list but said nothing about it, making a 6-member union look identical in TOON output to a genuine 4-member union. The fix (this shared helper) is exactly the enforcement `crates/core/AGENTS.md`'s design philosophy wants — a single named constructor/helper instead of parallel hand-copied logic.
120	
121	**Invariant 8:** Every `PropType` variant in `format_type_compact` that renders a bounded-length member list (currently a union of types and `Intersection`) must call `truncate_with_indicator` rather than hand-rolling its own `.join()`/slice logic. A new variant added later with the same "list of formatted members, potentially long" shape (e.g. if `Tuple` ever grows a compact-member rendering) should route through the same helper by default — don't reintroduce the exact bug this fix closed.
122	
123	**Invariant 9:** The `"...(+N)"` marker is a required, load-bearing signal, not decorative — `N` must be `parts.len() - limit`, i.e. the exact count of dropped members, not a placeholder or a boolean "more exist" flag. A consumer (LLM agent reading TOON context) uses `N` to judge whether the truncated tail is worth fetching via canonical JSON instead.
124	
125	### `format_type_compact` is a total function over `PropType` — no fallback arm
126	
127	Every `PropType` variant has an explicit match arm in `format_type_compact` (`toon.rs`) — there is no wildcard `_ => ...` catch-all. `PropType::Object(_)` and `PropType::Tuple(_)` delegate to `raw_string()` rather than a bespoke compact form (both can be arbitrarily nested/structured, so a hand-written compact form isn't obviously better than the existing raw renderer). `PropType::Opaque(detail)` renders as `opaque(<raw of the opaque detail>)`.
128	
129	**Invariant 10:** Adding a new `PropType` variant is a compile error in `format_type_compact` until a match arm is added (Rust's exhaustiveness check enforces this directly — no discipline required, the type system does it). Do not add a wildcard arm to silence that error; picking a deliberate compact representation for each new variant is the point.
130	
131	## JSON Schema export (`schema.rs`)
132	
133	### Hand-maintained, not derived
134	
135	`schema_value()` is a `serde_json::json!()` literal written by hand, describing `ExtractionOutput`'s shape for external tooling (editor integrations, validators) that want a JSON Schema rather than parsing Rust structs. It is explicitly **not** derived from the real structs via `schemars` or similar — Deriving it from the structs was proposed and never adopted (see "Locked design decision" below).
136	
137	### The drift-detection test's actual mechanism — targeted, not exhaustive
138	
139	`schema_covers_every_field_name_the_real_output_serializes` (`crates/cli/src/commands/schema.rs`) is the only guard against `schema_value()` silently falling out of sync with the real structs. Read honestly, its actual coverage boundary is narrower than "the schema matches the real output":
140	
141	1. It builds one hand-constructed `ExtractionOutput` fixture with one component (`Button`), one prop (`variant`), one inheritance layer, one diagnostic, and populated stats.
142	2. It serializes that fixture to a `serde_json::Value` and collects **field names only** (`obj.keys().cloned()`) from five specific nesting points: the component object itself, the `variant` prop object, the first inheritance-layer object, the first diagnostic object, and the `stats` object.
143	3. It stringifies the entire `schema_value()` output once (`serde_json::to_string`) and checks that every collected field name appears as a **substring** of that stringified schema (`!schema_str.contains(f.as_str())`).
144	
145	What this test catches: a field present in the real serialized output at one of those five specific object shapes, but whose name string never appears anywhere in the hand-written schema text — e.g. exactly the pre-fix drift (`.methods`/`.tags` and 5 of 9 `ExtractionStats` fields, `.line`/`.column`/`.help`).
146	
147	What this test does **not** catch, honestly stated:
148	
149	- **Nesting/placement correctness.** Because the check is `schema_str.contains(field_name)` over the _entire flattened schema string_, a field name appearing anywhere in the schema — even under a completely unrelated object — satisfies the check. A field accidentally documented under the wrong parent object would still pass.
150	- **Type correctness.** The test never checks that `schema_value()`'s declared `"type"` for a field matches the real field's serialized JSON type (string vs. object vs. array, etc.) — only that the name string exists somewhere.
151	- **Nested object shapes not walked by the fixture.** The fixture only descends into 5 specific paths (top-level component fields, the one prop, the one inheritance entry, the one diagnostic, stats). Fields nested deeper or differently — e.g. inside `notableInherited`'s value shape, or inside a prop's `tags`/`declarations`/`defaultValue` sub-objects — are never extracted from the fixture at all, so drift inside those substructures is invisible to this test.
152	- **Missing-field-in-real-output direction.** The test only checks "is every real field name present in the schema text," never the reverse ("does the schema claim a field that no longer exists in the real struct"). A schema field that's stale (renamed/removed on the Rust side) would not fail this test as long as no _other_ real field collides with its leftover name.
153	
154	Before the fix, the only existing test checked that the hand-written JSON was syntactically valid, never that it matched real serialized output. Now the test is better described as **targeted-but-shallow, not exhaustive** — it closes the specific "a whole field silently missing" failure mode for the object shapes it samples, but does not guarantee full recursive schema/struct parity.
155	
156	**Invariant 11:** Do not describe `schema_covers_every_field_name_the_real_output_serializes` as "verifying the schema matches the output" in any documentation or PR description — it verifies a narrower, specific property (field-name presence as a substring, at 5 sampled nesting depths) that happens to catch the historically-real drift bugs, not general schema/struct equivalence. If a future change needs stronger guarantees, that's the case for the proposed `schemars`-derived schema, not an argument that the current test is already sufficient.
157	
158	**Locked design decision:** the schema stays hand-written. Deriving `schemars::JsonSchema` on the plain output structs and hand-writing only `PropType`/`CollectedType`'s impls (mirroring ADR-0002's precedent of hand-writing `Serialize` for those same two recursive enums, to avoid a `schemars`/`serde` recursion-limit issue) was proposed and not adopted. `schema_value()` remains the hand-written source of truth for the exported schema, and the targeted-substring test above remains the only drift guard. Do not silently derive the schema for a subset of fields without either adopting the derive in full (with an ADR) or documenting a narrower interim decision — a half-derived, half-hand-written schema with no test coverage plan would be worse than the current fully-hand-written one.
159	
160	## Known gaps (cross-referenced, not re-derived)
161	
162	- **`ref`/`key` omission** — see Invariant 5 above; full quantification in `docs/benchmarks.md`.
163	- **Zero-member `LiteralUnion`/`Union`, upstream of serialization** — a zero-member `LiteralUnion` is reachable from several live construction paths (`known.rs`, `resolver/primitives.rs`, `resolver/alias.rs`, `resolver/mod.rs`, `resolver/template.rs`), cosmetic, not correctness-affecting. At the serialization layer specifically, Invariant 3's 2+ member guard already fully closes the "misleading `enum` shape" failure mode: a 0-member union fails `is_literal_union()`'s `>= 2` check, so `rdt::type_json` falls through to the plain `{"name": raw_string()}` branch, never `{"name": "enum", ...}`. The remaining gap is upstream of this document's scope — a 0-member union still renders as a not-very-useful empty-string raw type — and belongs to `resolver-type-resolution.md`, not this one.
164	- **JSON Schema drift, pre-fix history** — `.methods`/`.tags`, 5 of 9 `ExtractionStats` fields, `.line`/`.column`/`.help` were all previously undocumented in `schema.rs`; the drift-detection test now catches this specific class of regression (see coverage-boundary discussion above).
165	- **RDT `PropType` kind coverage matrix** — which `PropType` variants actually get exercised by which fixture is maintained in `docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s "PropType kinds" table; this document does not reproduce it. Notably, `void`/`never`/`any` are marked `❌ not covered` there for reasons unrelated to serialization (they're not realistic prop types in strict-mode real-world code), not because any serialization format mishandles them.
166

# Serialization formats

**Source:** `crates/core/src/pipeline/rdt.rs` (`serialize`, `docgen_info`, `type_json`, `omits`), `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs` (`serialize_rdt`), `crates/core/src/toon.rs` (whole module), `crates/cli/src/commands/schema.rs` (`schema_value`, `cmd_schema`, its drift test), `crates/core/src/types/output.rs` (`PropType::is_literal_union`), `crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs` (`ResolvedChain::give_up`, `empty_with_compose`)

This tool's canonical, lossless representation is `ExtractionOutput` — the struct tree in `crates/core/src/types/`, whose JSON writes each distinct prop once and refers to it by id (ADR 0009; see `types-and-output-contract.md`). Everything in this document is a _consumer-facing projection_ of that canonical form: two formats reshape it for specific downstream tools (`--format rdt`, `--format toon`), and one (`schema.rs`) describes its shape for external validators. None of the three is the source of truth; `ExtractionOutput` is.

## Schema version

The canonical JSON (`ExtractionOutput`, `IncrementalUpdate`, the session index) carries `schemaVersion` (ADR 0017); `SCHEMA_VERSION` in `crates/core/src/types/output.rs` is the one definition, and `schema.rs` requires it. Version 1 is the shape ADR 0009 describes. Version 2 (ADR 0018) writes a component's `props` as prop set ids, and an inheritance layer's `omitted` and a diagnostic's `affects` as name list ids, with `propSets` and `nameLists` tables beside `props`. Version 3 adds `optional` and `rest` to a function type's parameters, written only when true, and lists a rest parameter as the last parameter. OXC keeps `...rest` apart from the other parameters and the extractor read only the others, so `(...args: any[]) => void` printed as `() => void` and `(a?: string) => void` as `(a: string) => void`; a caller reading the signature believed an argument was required or that none were accepted. It is a bump, not an addition a reader can ignore: a version 2 reader would show `...args: any[]` as a required parameter named `args`. `raw_string` prints `a?: T` and `...a: T[]` as RDT does, TOON prints `T?` and `...T`, and `structural_hash` includes both flags. The TypeScript 7.1 backend does not set them: `crates/semantic/src/convert.rs` builds every parameter as required. Version 4 keeps three things the output used to drop, and is one bump because a version 3 reader would misread each: `readonly`, index signatures and the ref type's name. `readonly string[]` and `readonly [A, B]` are `{ "kind": "readonly", "element": … }` around the array or tuple (`PropType::Readonly`, `CollectedType::Readonly`); a union keeps `string[] | readonly string[]` as two members, since they are two types. An object field gains `readonly` (written only when true) for `readonly name: T`, and `indexKey` (written only for an index signature) for `[name: K]: T`: such a field is `name` the key parameter, `propType` the value and `indexKey` the key type. An index signature is not a prop, so everything that reads an object's fields as props, keys or lookup targets skips a field with `indexKey` (`is_member`), and a props type with only an index signature lists no props. `ref` gains `name`, the React type as written without `React.` (`Ref`, `RefObject`, `ForwardedRef`, `MutableRefObject`, `RefCallback`, `LegacyRef`, `ElementRef`), and `raw_string` prints `RefObject<T>` rather than `Ref<T>`. `declare const X: readonly ["a", "b"]` is still read as the tuple (`record_declared_value_type` peels the operator). The Vite plugin and the Storybook addon read version 4 only, and an old parse cache is discarded once (`CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` in `cache.rs`). The TypeScript 7.1 backend sets none of them: `crates/semantic/src/convert.rs` builds every object field as a plain, writable member and has no `readonly` or ref conversion. Not carried: `readonly` on a component's own props (a `readonly label: string` member of a props interface), which no consumer reads yet. A collapsed inheritance layer (`docs/architecture/resolver-type-resolution.md`, Collapse) also names the props it holds: `InheritedLayer.members`, written as the id of a list in `nameLists` (so a source shared by many components is written once) and only for a layer that has members. It is an addition a reader can ignore, so it did not move `SCHEMA_VERSION`; a reader that wants to know whether a prop collapsed away or is absent reads it.

- **Bump** when a reader of the previous version would misread or lose data: a field removed, renamed or retyped, its meaning changed, or references and tables restructured. A new field, a new `detectedBy` value or a new diagnostic code is not a bump; readers must tolerate them.
- **A bump ships** in a changeset marked breaking for the core crate and every package that reads the JSON.
- **Readers** (`ExtractionOutput`'s `Deserialize`, `packages/vite-plugin/src/schema.ts`, `packages/storybook/src/schema.ts`) accept their own version, reject any other with an error naming both, and read output with no `schemaVersion` as version 1.
- `--format rdt`, `--format storybook` and `--format toon` carry no version; they have other tools' shapes. The parse cache has its own `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`.

## Where this code lives, and why that's not a AGENTS.md violation

`crates/core/AGENTS.md` says "no terminal/display code in `crates/core`." The RDT projection (`pipeline/rdt.rs`) and `toon.rs` (`render_output_toon`, `render_component_toon`, `format_type_compact`) live in **`crates/core`**, and both are serialization formats, not extraction logic.

The line the project actually draws, reverse-engineered from where each format lives: "terminal/display code" means code whose job is to _render for a human looking at a terminal_ (colors, tables, spinners — `crates/cli/src/output.rs`'s comfy-table helpers, `indicatif` progress bars). A _serialization format_ — even a human-readable, LLM-optimized one like TOON — is a consumer-facing data contract, judged by "does another program or prompt consume this," not "is it pretty-printed." TOON is core-side because it's plumbed through `PipelineOptions`/pipeline output the same way canonical JSON is (`caliper_docgen_core::toon::render_output_toon(&output)` called from `cmd_extract` in `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs`), and because a NAPI/plugin consumer could plausibly want TOON output too, not just the CLI. The RDT shape is core-side for the same reason: the NAPI binding's `sessionDocgenInfo` returns it per component for the Storybook provider (`packages/storybook`), and `--format rdt` (`serialize_rdt`) delegates to the same module.

**Invariant 1:** A new serialization format belongs in `crates/core` only if a non-CLI consumer (NAPI binding, a plugin, a future query server) could plausibly want to produce it directly from a `PipelineOptions`/`ExtractionOutput` value. If a format exists solely to match another CLI tool's file-format contract, it belongs in `crates/cli/src/commands/`, not `crates/core`.

## RDT format (`pipeline::rdt`)

Two entry points share one projection: `serialize` (`--format rdt`) applies RDT's default `skipChildrenPropWithoutDoc` (`omits`), and `docgen_info` (the NAPI `sessionDocgenInfo`, feeding the Storybook provider) keeps an undocumented `children`, because Storybook 11's React docgen lists it.

`serialize` holds only components with `exported: true`, unless `--include-unexported` is passed. react-docgen-typescript documents only a module's exports, so a file-local helper component would otherwise appear in RDT-shaped output where RDT never puts one.

Each component `serialize` writes carries `filePath`, the absolute path of its source file, as RDT's `ComponentDoc` does. `docgen_info` leaves it out.

### The `enum`-shape convention (`type_json`)

react-docgen-typescript encodes a literal union prop type not as an inlined string but as a structured shape renderers pattern-match on:

```rust
if prop_type.is_literal_union() {
    let values: Vec<serde_json::Value> = match prop_type {
        PropType::Union(members) => members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": m.raw_string()})).collect(),
        PropType::LiteralUnion { members, .. } => {
            members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": format!("\"{m}\"")})).collect()
        }
        single => vec![serde_json::json!({"value": single.raw_string()})],
    };
    return serde_json::json!({ "name": "enum", "raw": prop_type.raw_string(), "value": values });
}
serde_json::json!({ "name": prop_type.raw_string() })
```

A single string or number literal (`kind?: 'button'`) is a one-option `enum`, which is what Storybook's own docgen produces for it. A union with a boolean member (`'a' | 1 | true`) is not an `enum`: Storybook unquotes each option's source text into a string or a number, so `true` would reach the control as the string `"true"`. It stays a type name, `{"name": "\"a\" | 1 | true"}`, which Storybook's converter splits at the `|` and parses as JSON itself, giving the options `["a", 1, true]` with a real boolean (its own docgen gives such a union no options at all). That holds only while every member's text survives the split and parse: a string holding `|`, `"` or `\` (`'a|b' | true`) is split inside the literal or fails `JSON.parse` (`'a\\b'` parses to a backspace), and Storybook then picks an `object` control. Such a union is an `enum` as before (`true` is then the string "true"), so that no option is lost.

This exists because Storybook's own docgen addon (a real consumer of RDT's JSON) looks for `type.name === "enum"` as the trigger to render a `<select>` control instead of a free-text field — the single highest-value renderer hook for the most commonly curated kind of prop in any design system (`variant`, `size`, `color`, …).

**Invariant 2:** `rdt::type_json` returns `{"name": "enum", "raw": ..., "value": [...]}` if and only if `prop_type.is_literal_union()` is `true`. Do not special-case `PropType::Union`/`PropType::LiteralUnion` shape-matching directly inside `rdt::type_json` — route every literal-union check through `is_literal_union()`, because that's the single place that rule (below) is enforced.

### Which types are `enum`s

`PropType::is_literal_union()` (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`) is true for a non-empty `Union` whose members are all string or number literals, a `Union` of literals with at least one string or number and a boolean whose text Storybook cannot split and parse from the type name (`reads_as_json_options`), a non-empty `LiteralUnion`, and a lone string or number literal (a bare `StringLiteral`/`NumberLiteral`).

**Invariant 3:** A `PropType::Union`/`PropType::LiteralUnion` with **0** members, and a union of booleans only (a lone `true` included), is never reported as an `enum` shape. An empty "enum" (`{"name": "enum", "value": []}`) is misleading to a prop-table renderer, and a zero-member `LiteralUnion` is still reachable (if cosmetic) from several construction paths (`known.rs`, `resolver/primitives.rs`, `resolver/alias.rs`, `resolver/mod.rs`, `resolver/template.rs`); the guard in `is_literal_union()` keeps that from surfacing as a broken `enum` shape in RDT output, where it degrades to a plain `{"name": raw_string()}`. A single string or number literal is an enum: before, it was written as a type name, and Storybook picked an `object` control for a prop that is only ever `'button'`.

### `@ignore`

`component_doc` leaves out a prop whose tags hold `ignore`, in both `serialize` and `docgen_info`, because Storybook's own docgen (`@storybook/react`'s `react-component-meta` path) drops `@ignore` props and no other tag (`@internal`, `@private`, `@hidden` and `@deprecated` props are all listed). The canonical output keeps the prop and its tag.

### `composes` reused for the resolver's give-up cases

RDT natively supports a `composes: string[]` field on each component — "these props come from this named type, listed by reference, not flattened into `props`." This tool's resolver reuses that exact mechanism for a second, distinct purpose: recording every type it gave up trying to resolve. `ResolvedChain::give_up` (`crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs`) is "the sanctioned 'give up' entry point for every 'this type couldn't be followed further, stop here' path" — it pushes an optional `Diagnostic` and then calls `empty_with_compose(type_name)`, which sets `composes: vec![type_name]`. Every unresolvable type (a conditional type, a generic pattern the resolver doesn't understand, a cycle) lands in `composes` instead of silently vanishing from `props`.

`rdt::docgen_info` passes `entry.composes` straight through (`"composes": entry.composes`) — this was previously a real bug (see `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs`'s `rdt_output_includes_composes` test and its docstring): the resolver populated `composes` correctly but `serialize_rdt` silently dropped it from the emitted JSON. Fixed; the field now round-trips.

**Invariant 4:** `composes` in the emitted RDT JSON carries two semantically different populations that are _not_ distinguished from each other in the output: (a) types RDT itself would put there — legitimate "props come from elsewhere" composition, and (b) types this resolver gave up resolving. A consumer reading `composes` cannot tell which case produced a given entry without re-running extraction and checking `diagnostics` for a correlated warning. Do not "clean up" `give_up` to stop populating `composes`, and do not add a second field to split the two populations without updating this doc and `resolver-type-resolution.md` — the reuse is intentional (see that file for the resolver-side rationale), not an accident that happens to also serialize correctly.

**Cross-reference:** the resolver-side mechanics of `give_up`/`empty_with_compose`/cycle detection belong to `resolver-type-resolution.md`, not here — this file only documents the serialization-format consequence (the field showing up in RDT JSON), not the resolution logic that populates it.

### `ref`/`key`: deliberate omission, not a bug, not relocated

RDT lists React's `ref` and `key` reconciliation props alongside a component's real props. This tool does not. `docs/benchmarks.md` documents this precisely: of components with any prop-count mismatch against real RDT, "the other 24 (0.9%, spread across 12 of the other 23 components) are **100% `ref`/`key`**... Worth being precise about that one: it's an omission, not a relocation — this tool doesn't surface forwardRef/ref-type metadata anywhere else either (checked `ComponentEntry`'s full field list — no such field exists), so 'we chose not to add it' is accurate, but 'the same info lives elsewhere' isn't."

**Invariant 5:** Neither `ref` nor `key` appears in `props`, in any other `ComponentEntry` field, or in any of the serialization formats in this document. If a future change adds `ref`-as-prop support (React 19's `function Button({ ref, ...props })` pattern — see `docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s "React 19 `ref`-as-prop" note, already investigated and found to already work structurally when `ref` is an explicit member of the props type), that is a change to what the _resolver_ extracts, not a serialization-format decision — this document's job is only to record that today, none of the formats invent `ref`/`key` entries that the canonical `ExtractionOutput` doesn't already contain.

### `methods: []` — always empty, and why RDT/Storybook both still carry the field

**Locked design decision:** `rdt::docgen_info` hardcodes `"methods": []` unconditionally rather than omitting the field or computing it. This tool does not extract class component methods — "this tool doesn't extract class methods, and RDT consumers (Storybook's docgen addon) only ever read it for class components". Since class components are explicitly out of scope for this project (`docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s Component patterns table: `Class component | ❌ | out of scope (modern React only)`), the field is kept present-but-empty rather than dropped, because RDT/Storybook consumers may assume the key always exists on a valid RDT-shaped component entry — dropping it risks a `TypeError` on `.methods.length` in a consumer that doesn't defensively check for the key's presence, whereas an empty array is always safe to iterate.

## TOON format (`crates/core/src/toon.rs`)

TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) is a compact, indentation-and-CSV-like text encoding for `ExtractionOutput`, designed for LLM prompt/agent-context consumption rather than for a program to parse back into structured data.

### It is deliberately lossy — not meant to round-trip

**Locked design decision:** TOON output is not a serialization format in the reversible sense. It:

- Collapses `PropType` into a single compact string per prop (`format_type_compact`) — e.g. `Array<string>`, `Ref<HTMLButtonElement>`, `(event: MouseEvent) => void`, `opaque(CustomType)` — discarding structure a JSON consumer would get from the tagged `PropType` enum (no way to tell from the string alone whether `SxProps` came from `PropType::SxProps` vs. a `Named` type happening to render the same text).
- Escapes only for CSV-safety (`escape_toon_val`: commas, newlines, quotes) — not for full round-trip fidelity.
- Truncates a union of types (more than 8 members), an intersection (more than 4) and a collapsed layer's `members` (more than 24), replacing the tail with a `"...(+N)"` marker; the canonical JSON holds every member. It never cuts a literal union or a union with a literal member, because an agent writes a call from those values. A function type keeps its parameter names. A prop's `@deprecated`, `@see` and `@since` tags are written in a `tags` column (present only when some prop has one), and a discriminated union's discriminant prop in a `discriminant:` line.

There is no `parse_toon` / deserializer anywhere in the codebase, and none is planned — TOON is a one-way export.

**Invariant 7:** No code path may treat TOON output as re-parseable back into `ExtractionOutput` or any `PropType`. If a future feature needs a compact-but-lossless format, that is a new format, not an extension of TOON's contract.

### Truncation with a required indicator — recently made consistent

`truncate_with_indicator(parts: &[String], limit: usize, sep: &str) -> String` (`crates/core/src/toon.rs`) is the single shared helper for "cut a member list down to `limit` items, and if anything was cut, say so":

```rust
fn truncate_with_indicator(parts: &[String], limit: usize, sep: &str) -> String {
    if parts.len() <= limit {
        return parts.join(sep);
    }
    let mut shown: Vec<String> = parts[..limit].to_vec();
    shown.push(format!("...(+{})", parts.len() - limit));
    shown.join(sep)
}
```

Three call sites route through it, each with its own cap: `Union` of types only (`UNION_LIMIT` 8, separator `|`; a union with a string, number or boolean literal member is written in full), `Intersection` (limit 4, separator `&`) and a layer's `members` (limit 24). `LiteralUnion` is not cut.

This was a real, confirmed bug before the fix: `LiteralUnion`'s truncate-with-indicator logic existed but was never factored into a shared helper, so when `Union`/`Intersection` needed the same behavior _in the same function_ (`format_type_compact`), the indicator half was silently dropped — those two branches truncated the member list but said nothing about it, making a 6-member union look identical in TOON output to a genuine 4-member union. The fix (this shared helper) is exactly the enforcement `crates/core/AGENTS.md`'s design philosophy wants — a single named constructor/helper instead of parallel hand-copied logic.

**Invariant 8:** Every `PropType` variant in `format_type_compact` that renders a bounded-length member list (currently a union of types and `Intersection`) must call `truncate_with_indicator` rather than hand-rolling its own `.join()`/slice logic. A new variant added later with the same "list of formatted members, potentially long" shape (e.g. if `Tuple` ever grows a compact-member rendering) should route through the same helper by default — don't reintroduce the exact bug this fix closed.

**Invariant 9:** The `"...(+N)"` marker is a required, load-bearing signal, not decorative — `N` must be `parts.len() - limit`, i.e. the exact count of dropped members, not a placeholder or a boolean "more exist" flag. A consumer (LLM agent reading TOON context) uses `N` to judge whether the truncated tail is worth fetching via canonical JSON instead.

### `format_type_compact` is a total function over `PropType` — no fallback arm

Every `PropType` variant has an explicit match arm in `format_type_compact` (`toon.rs`) — there is no wildcard `_ => ...` catch-all. `PropType::Object(_)` and `PropType::Tuple(_)` delegate to `raw_string()` rather than a bespoke compact form (both can be arbitrarily nested/structured, so a hand-written compact form isn't obviously better than the existing raw renderer). `PropType::Opaque(detail)` renders as `opaque(<raw of the opaque detail>)`.

**Invariant 10:** Adding a new `PropType` variant is a compile error in `format_type_compact` until a match arm is added (Rust's exhaustiveness check enforces this directly — no discipline required, the type system does it). Do not add a wildcard arm to silence that error; picking a deliberate compact representation for each new variant is the point.

## JSON Schema export (`schema.rs`)

### Hand-maintained, not derived

`schema_value()` is a `serde_json::json!()` literal written by hand, describing `ExtractionOutput`'s shape for external tooling (editor integrations, validators) that want a JSON Schema rather than parsing Rust structs. It is explicitly **not** derived from the real structs via `schemars` or similar — Deriving it from the structs was proposed and never adopted (see "Locked design decision" below).

### The drift-detection test's actual mechanism — targeted, not exhaustive

`schema_covers_every_field_name_the_real_output_serializes` (`crates/cli/src/commands/schema.rs`) is the only guard against `schema_value()` silently falling out of sync with the real structs. Read honestly, its actual coverage boundary is narrower than "the schema matches the real output":

1. It builds one hand-constructed `ExtractionOutput` fixture with one component (`Button`), one prop (`variant`), one inheritance layer, one diagnostic, and populated stats.
2. It serializes that fixture to a `serde_json::Value` and collects **field names only** (`obj.keys().cloned()`) from five specific nesting points: the component object itself, the `variant` prop object, the first inheritance-layer object, the first diagnostic object, and the `stats` object.
3. It stringifies the entire `schema_value()` output once (`serde_json::to_string`) and checks that every collected field name appears as a **substring** of that stringified schema (`!schema_str.contains(f.as_str())`).

What this test catches: a field present in the real serialized output at one of those five specific object shapes, but whose name string never appears anywhere in the hand-written schema text — e.g. exactly the pre-fix drift (`.methods`/`.tags` and 5 of 9 `ExtractionStats` fields, `.line`/`.column`/`.help`).

What this test does **not** catch, honestly stated:

- **Nesting/placement correctness.** Because the check is `schema_str.contains(field_name)` over the _entire flattened schema string_, a field name appearing anywhere in the schema — even under a completely unrelated object — satisfies the check. A field accidentally documented under the wrong parent object would still pass.
- **Type correctness.** The test never checks that `schema_value()`'s declared `"type"` for a field matches the real field's serialized JSON type (string vs. object vs. array, etc.) — only that the name string exists somewhere.
- **Nested object shapes not walked by the fixture.** The fixture only descends into 5 specific paths (top-level component fields, the one prop, the one inheritance entry, the one diagnostic, stats). Fields nested deeper or differently — e.g. inside `notableInherited`'s value shape, or inside a prop's `tags`/`declarations`/`defaultValue` sub-objects — are never extracted from the fixture at all, so drift inside those substructures is invisible to this test.
- **Missing-field-in-real-output direction.** The test only checks "is every real field name present in the schema text," never the reverse ("does the schema claim a field that no longer exists in the real struct"). A schema field that's stale (renamed/removed on the Rust side) would not fail this test as long as no _other_ real field collides with its leftover name.

Before the fix, the only existing test checked that the hand-written JSON was syntactically valid, never that it matched real serialized output. Now the test is better described as **targeted-but-shallow, not exhaustive** — it closes the specific "a whole field silently missing" failure mode for the object shapes it samples, but does not guarantee full recursive schema/struct parity.

**Invariant 11:** Do not describe `schema_covers_every_field_name_the_real_output_serializes` as "verifying the schema matches the output" in any documentation or PR description — it verifies a narrower, specific property (field-name presence as a substring, at 5 sampled nesting depths) that happens to catch the historically-real drift bugs, not general schema/struct equivalence. If a future change needs stronger guarantees, that's the case for the proposed `schemars`-derived schema, not an argument that the current test is already sufficient.

**Locked design decision:** the schema stays hand-written. Deriving `schemars::JsonSchema` on the plain output structs and hand-writing only `PropType`/`CollectedType`'s impls (mirroring ADR-0002's precedent of hand-writing `Serialize` for those same two recursive enums, to avoid a `schemars`/`serde` recursion-limit issue) was proposed and not adopted. `schema_value()` remains the hand-written source of truth for the exported schema, and the targeted-substring test above remains the only drift guard. Do not silently derive the schema for a subset of fields without either adopting the derive in full (with an ADR) or documenting a narrower interim decision — a half-derived, half-hand-written schema with no test coverage plan would be worse than the current fully-hand-written one.

## Known gaps (cross-referenced, not re-derived)

- **`ref`/`key` omission** — see Invariant 5 above; full quantification in `docs/benchmarks.md`.
- **Zero-member `LiteralUnion`/`Union`, upstream of serialization** — a zero-member `LiteralUnion` is reachable from several live construction paths (`known.rs`, `resolver/primitives.rs`, `resolver/alias.rs`, `resolver/mod.rs`, `resolver/template.rs`), cosmetic, not correctness-affecting. At the serialization layer specifically, Invariant 3's 2+ member guard already fully closes the "misleading `enum` shape" failure mode: a 0-member union fails `is_literal_union()`'s `>= 2` check, so `rdt::type_json` falls through to the plain `{"name": raw_string()}` branch, never `{"name": "enum", ...}`. The remaining gap is upstream of this document's scope — a 0-member union still renders as a not-very-useful empty-string raw type — and belongs to `resolver-type-resolution.md`, not this one.
- **JSON Schema drift, pre-fix history** — `.methods`/`.tags`, 5 of 9 `ExtractionStats` fields, `.line`/`.column`/`.help` were all previously undocumented in `schema.rs`; the drift-detection test now catches this specific class of regression (see coverage-boundary discussion above).
- **RDT `PropType` kind coverage matrix** — which `PropType` variants actually get exercised by which fixture is maintained in `docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s "PropType kinds" table; this document does not reproduce it. Notably, `void`/`never`/`any` are marked `❌ not covered` there for reasons unrelated to serialization (they're not realistic prop types in strict-mode real-world code), not because any serialization format mishandles them.

This is the resolver's entire job, structurally: eliminate every "can't be sure yet" variant.

55	## LOCKED DESIGN DECISION: manual Serialize/Deserialize on the recursive enums (ADR-0002)
56	
57	**Source:** `docs/adr/0002-manual-serialize-for-prop-type.md`
58	
59	`PropType` and `CollectedType` do **not** derive `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Both implement the serde traits by hand. `CollectedType` (`crates/core/src/types/collected.rs`) round-trips through a private `to_json_value`/`from_json_value` pair that builds and reads a `serde_json::Value`. `PropType` (`crates/core/src/types/output.rs`) streams its `Serialize` impl straight into the serializer as a map with `kind` first and the fields in a fixed order (an `OpaqueReason` is written by the private `WireReason` as `{ type, ... }`), and deserializes through a private `from_tagged_value` over a `serde_json::Value`.
60	
61	**Why:** these are recursive enums (`Union(Vec<Self>)`, `Object(Vec<Field>)` where `Field` contains `Self`, `Array(Box<Self>)`, ...). A derived, tagged (`#[serde(tag = "kind")]`) implementation on a recursive enum needed `#![recursion_limit = "2048"]` to compile — each nesting level wraps the generated (de)serializer in another codegen layer, and a real component prop tree blows past the default limit (128). Manual impls sidestep the codegen recursion entirely; they're just recursive Rust functions, which the compiler doesn't limit the same way.
62	
63	**Do not "simplify" this back to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`.** It looks removable — it's a lot of boilerplate for something serde could theoretically generate — but doing so reintroduces the recursion-limit dependency, and worse, silently drops the manual NaN/Infinity handling described below.
64	
65	**Correction to the ADR itself, verified against current code:** ADR-0002 states "`PropType`, `CollectedType`, and `OpaqueReason` don't derive Serialize/Deserialize." This is stale for `OpaqueReason`. The current source (`OpaqueReason` in `types/output.rs`) shows:
66	
67	```rust
68	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
69	#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
70	pub enum OpaqueReason {
71	    ConditionalType, MappedType, ModuleAugmentation,
72	    RuntimeDependent { function_name: String },
73	    UnresolvableImport { specifier: String },
74	    PandaCodegenMissing, DepthExceeded,
75	    IndexedAccess { expression: String },
76	    TemplateLiteral { expression: String },
77	    UnsupportedExpression,
78	}
79	```
80	
81	`OpaqueReason` derives normally. It isn't recursive — every variant's payload is a `String` or a unit — so it never hit the recursion-limit problem the ADR is about. The _serialization of an `OpaqueReason` value_ is still hand-assembled by `WireReason` (`types/output.rs`, matching each reason to its own `{ type, ... }` shape) when `PropType`'s `Serialize` writes the `Opaque` variant, and hand-parsed in `PropType::from_tagged_value` — but that's because it's embedded inside `PropType`'s own manual impl, not because `OpaqueReason` itself needs one. This is a small, real documentation bug in ADR-0002 worth a one-line fix, independent of anything else in this file.
82	
83	Also worth noting as **resolved, not a gap:** the ADR flagged `#![recursion_limit = "2048"]` in `lib.rs` as "left over from the old derive-based design... worth deleting as a follow-up." As of the current source, `crates/core/src/lib.rs` has no `recursion_limit` attribute at all — that follow-up has already happened. The ADR's "Consequences" section is stale on this point too.
84	
85	### The "no wildcard matches" convention
86	
87	**Invariant 1:** Every match on `PropType` or `CollectedType` inside the manual serde impls, and by extension idiomatically everywhere else in the resolver, must be exhaustive — no `_ => ...` fallthrough arm.
88	
89	**Why it's load-bearing:** a derived serde impl gives you a compiler error the moment you add a new enum variant and forget to handle it in serialization. A hand-written match loses that safety net _unless every match stays exhaustive_ — a wildcard arm would silently absorb a new variant into whatever the wildcard does (often `Opaque` or a panic), and nothing would tell you serialization is now lossy for that variant. `PropType`'s `Serialize` impl and `from_tagged_value` (`types/output.rs`), and `to_json_value`/`from_json_value` in `collected.rs`, are all written this way. If you add a `PropType` variant, the compiler _will_ fail the exhaustiveness check in the `Serialize` impl and force you to handle it — but only because nobody put a wildcard there. Adding one defeats the entire safety mechanism this ADR relies on.

91	### NaN/Infinity as a wire-format special case
92	
93	**Invariant 2:** `PropType::NumberLiteral(f64)` and `CollectedType::NumberLiteral(f64)` encode non-finite values (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`) as JSON strings (`"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`), not as JSON numbers, and the read side must check for a string before falling back to `as_f64()`.
94	
95	**Why:** `serde_json::Number` (and JSON itself) cannot represent non-finite floats — `serde_json::json!(f64::NAN)` silently becomes `null`. Both files have explicit round-trip tests for this (`number_literal_roundtrip_tests` in `output.rs`, the NaN/Infinity/-Infinity tests in `collected.rs`'s `mod tests`) — treat those as regression guards, not optional coverage.
